segments.text: The Civil Rights Movement combined courts, grassroots activists, national leaders, media, and federal government together — it cannot be reduced to a single leader’s biography, however important Martin Luther King Jr. was to specific episodes.

items.text: The Supreme Court decision declaring school segregation unconstitutional, though implementation was slow and resisted.
Prepare the movement as a combination of courts, grassroots activists, national leaders, media, federal government and local resistance; avoid making one famous leader the entire story.
Do not make Martin Luther King Jr. the entire movement.
Do not say Brown immediately integrated all schools; resistance was extensive and implementation was slow.
Do not treat passage of the 1964 and 1965 laws as the end of racial inequality.
Brown v. Board of Education (1954) declared school segregation unconstitutional.
The Montgomery bus boycott (1955–56) and the March on Washington (1963) were major movement milestones.
The Civil Rights Act (1964) and Voting Rights Act (1965) targeted discrimination and voting barriers respectively.
Present civil rights as a broad movement with legal, grassroots, and political dimensions together — never a biography of one leader.
Legal victories (1954, 1964, 1965) mark essential milestones, not the end point, of the struggle for racial equality.
